choices.text: Reference it in the job with `${resources.experiments.churn_exp.id}`, which the bundle resolves at deployment
Let the job create a new experiment with a random name on every run and ignore the one the bundle declared
Look the experiment up by its display name in a notebook cell and skip all bundle configuration
Hard-code the ID of the experiment in the job after the first deployment, and deploy twice

stem: A governed table `ml.crm.customer_dim` is fully rewritten every night by a pipeline. It has no event timestamp that describes when a row happened, and it holds no model predictions. The team wants data quality metrics, such as null rates and distributions, tracked for each nightly state of the whole table. Which profile type fits?

choices.text: An inference profile with the customer id as the model id column, so that every customer is profiled as a separate model
No profile at all, because profiles can be attached only to tables that grow by appending rows and never to rewritten tables
A snapshot profile, which processes the complete table at every refresh and records the metrics for the state of the table at that time
A time series profile on the `updated_at` column, with a daily granularity, so that each nightly rewrite becomes a separate time window

stem: A serving endpoint logs requests and responses to an inference table. The request and response columns hold JSON strings with the feature values and the prediction, and true labels arrive later in a separate table. The team wants an inference profile with accuracy and F1 trends. What should the pipeline do before the profile is created?

choices.text: Create a time series profile on the logged table, because inference profiles accept only tables written by batch scoring jobs and never endpoint logs, and it would give the same metrics
Schedule a job that unpacks the JSON into one column per feature and prediction, joins the labels and creates the profile on the resulting Delta table
Export the table to a CSV file in a volume every night, because profiles are able to read only files and cannot read Delta tables
Create the inference profile directly on the logged table and set the prediction column to the response JSON column, which the profile parses automatically

stem: A team creates a time series profile today on an events table that has two years of history, expecting two years of daily metrics. The first refresh finishes, but the dashboard shows only about the last month. No error is reported. What explains this?

choices.text: The daily granularity discards all windows older than the retention period of the metric tables, which is set to 30 days by default in the profile
The profile processes only the files added since the table was last optimized, and the older files are skipped until a full refresh is requested
The dashboard was created by a different user, and Unity Catalog row filters hide the older windows from everyone except the table owner
When a time series or inference profile is created, only the data from the 30 days before its creation is analyzed; new data is processed after that

stem: A 6TB append-only table of clickstream events, with an `event_ts` timestamp, must be profiled for null rates and distribution drift. A first attempt with a snapshot profile is rejected for size. Refresh cost must also stay low as the table grows. Which configuration meets both needs?

choices.text: A time series profile on `event_ts` with change data feed enabled on the table, so that each refresh processes only newly appended data
An inference profile, because it supports larger tables than snapshot and does not require predictions when the label column is omitted
A snapshot profile on a deep clone refreshed monthly, which keeps the profiled table under the limit while the source continues to grow
A snapshot profile with a slicing expression on `event_ts`, so that each slice is smaller than the maximum table size for snapshots

stem: A platform team has already attached a snapshot profile to `ml.churn.scored_customers`. An ML engineer now tries to create an inference profile on the same table through the API to get accuracy trends, and the call fails. The table does have prediction, label, timestamp and model version columns. What is the correct way forward?

choices.text: Delete the snapshot profile, or profile a separate view or table over the same predictions, because a table can have only one profile
Ask for the MANAGE privilege on the catalog, because creating an additional profile on a table needs a privilege higher than the first one
Create the second profile with a different output schema, because the limit applies to each metric-table location and not to the table
Add inference settings to the existing snapshot profile with an update call, because one profile can combine the snapshot and inference types

stem: An ML engineer holds SELECT on `ml.churn.scored_customers`, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its catalog and schema. Creating a data profile on that table through the API still fails with a permission error. The engineer is not a metastore admin. Which additional privilege resolves it?

choices.text: CREATE MODEL on the schema, because every inference profile registers a small monitoring model there while it is created
MANAGE on the catalog, the schema or the table, which completes the privileges that data profiling requires
Membership in the workspace admins group, because profiles can be created on a table only by workspace administrators
MODIFY on the table, because the profile appends its metric rows back into the profiled table as additional partitions

stem: To profile an endpoint's request log, a team defines a materialized view that unpacks the JSON payloads and joins the labels, and attaches a time series profile to that view. As the log grows, every refresh of the profile takes longer, although only one day of new rows arrives each time. What explains this, and what is the fix?

choices.text: Change data feed is honored only by snapshot profiles, so a time series profile always reprocesses the table; recreate the profile as a snapshot profile
Profiles cannot be attached to views of any kind, so the profile silently scans the source inference table instead; export the unpacked rows to CSV files and profile those files
Materialized views get no incremental processing, so each refresh re-reads everything; append the unpacked log to a Delta table with change data feed and profile that table
The profile repeats its 30-day look-back at every refresh, so the run time keeps rising; ask for a longer look-back so that each refresh covers the whole history once

stem: An inference profile is refreshing on schedule and the drift tables fill normally, but the accuracy, precision and recall columns are NULL for every window. The prediction column is configured. Which cause is most likely?

choices.text: The model was registered in Unity Catalog instead of the workspace registry, which blocks the quality metrics of an inference profile
The profile is set to a daily granularity, and quality metrics are computed only for windows of one week or longer
The drift metrics are computed first and block the quality metrics until baseline drift has been calculated for each column
No label column is configured, or the ground-truth labels were never joined to the logged predictions, so model quality cannot be calculated

stem: A data scientist created an inference profile. The risk team has no other access to the schema, but must read the profile metrics and drift metrics tables and wants to build its own SQL alerts on them. How is that access controlled?

choices.text: Access follows the profile's notification settings, so the emails listed per event type are the principals allowed to query the tables
The metric tables count as system tables that every workspace user can read automatically, so the risk team needs no grant at all to query them
The creator owns the metric tables, and the risk team gets Unity Catalog privileges such as SELECT, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA
Only the dashboard can be shared; the tables behind it cannot be granted, so the risk team needs a nightly copy of them in its own schema

stem: A customer complains that the endpoint returned a nonsensical score for one specific request yesterday. The ML engineer needs the exact input payload and response, the HTTP status code and the execution time of that single request. Which monitoring component holds that detail?

choices.text: The inference table of the endpoint, which logs request and response payloads with status codes and timing in a Unity Catalog Delta table
The aggregated profile metrics table, which stores the raw payload of every request for each time window
The Model Registry page of the model version, which keeps a copy of each scored request for 90 days
The dashboard created by the profile, which can be filtered down to one single request with the request id widget of its filter bar

stem: A regulated team must keep system logs, custom application logs, metrics and traces of a custom model serving endpoint for years, queryable with SQL. The endpoint health metrics in the Serving UI are only available for the last 14 days. Which approach meets the retention requirement?

choices.text: Take a screenshot of the Serving UI charts every week and store the images in a volume together with the audit documents
Configure OpenTelemetry telemetry on the endpoint so that logs, metrics and traces persist to Unity Catalog Delta tables for long-term retention
Keep only the ephemeral service logs, because stdout and stderr streams are stored in the logs tab of the endpoint without any time limit
Increase the granularity of the profile to one year so that the metric tables keep the endpoint logs for that period

stem: After the nightly profile refresh succeeds, business stakeholders who open the profile dashboard in the morning still see last week's charts. The metric tables already contain the new windows. What is the cause and the fix?

choices.text: Dashboards read the baseline table only, so the new windows appear after the baseline table is replaced by the latest data
The profile refresh also needs a manual publish of the dashboard, and only the profile owner can publish it for other users as well
The metric tables sit in another catalog than the dashboard reads, so the output schema must change
The dashboard refreshes separately from the profile, so its queries must run again after the profile refresh, for example on a schedule

stem: The on-call team wants a Slack or PagerDuty notification when the population stability index of any numeric feature of a served model exceeds an agreed threshold. The drift metrics table is refreshed daily by the profile. Which design implements this with documented features?

choices.text: Run a notebook every hour that reads the dashboard widgets and posts a message to the channel with a webhook
Add the on-call address to the profile's email notification setting, which sends a message whenever any drift metric crosses a threshold
Set the endpoint's rate limit to the threshold, so that requests are refused when the drift of the inputs is too large
Create a Databricks SQL query on the drift metrics table and an alert on it with a notification destination such as a webhook, Slack or PagerDuty

stem: A team configured email addresses in the profile's notification settings, and expected an email when feature drift increased last week. Drift was clearly visible in the drift metrics table but nobody was notified. What is the reason?

choices.text: The email limit was exceeded, because a profile sends at most one email per week for each monitored column
Emails are sent only for baseline drift, and the profile had no baseline table, so none were generated
The notification settings cover events such as a failed or timed-out refresh and never check drift values; drift needs a SQL alert on the drift table
Notifications work only for snapshot profiles, so the inference profile could not send any email about drift, whatever the thresholds in the metric tables were

stem: An inference profile covers a model with 120 features. Alerting on each feature separately would create 120 alert objects to own and tune, and a single event can shift many features together. Which design gives the team a manageable but still specific alert?

choices.text: One alert whose query returns the columns whose drift against the baseline is above the agreed threshold in the latest window, firing if any row comes back
One alert on the average of all drift values across the 120 columns, which hides a single strongly drifting feature in the mean
One alert on the number of rows in the profile metrics table, because a new window is written only when some feature has drifted
120 alerts created by script, one per feature, each with its own destination and threshold, because a query is unable to group several features together

stem: A SQL alert was built from a dashboard query on the drift metrics table, with the query parameter `:model_id` whose default is 1. After version 2 replaced version 1 in production, the alert never fires although version 2 inputs drifted. What should the team check?

choices.text: The size of the baseline table, because drift for a new model version is computed only if the baseline has at least one million rows
The default parameter value, because an alert based on a query with parameters uses the default values, so it still evaluates version 1
The refresh history of the dashboard, because alerts are evaluated only after someone opens the dashboard
The notification destination, because alerts on parameterized queries send messages only to the query owner

stem: A monitoring owner worries that the drift alert would stay silent if the profile stopped refreshing, for example after a schedule was disabled or the refresh failed repeatedly. Which design closes this gap?

choices.text: Add a freshness alert on the metric tables (latest window end older than expected) and set the profile's failure notification
Remove the profile schedule and refresh it only on demand, so that no scheduled run can fail silently
Rely on the existing drift alert, because it also evaluates to true whenever no new rows are found in the drift metrics table
Increase the alert evaluation frequency to every minute, which forces the profile to refresh when the alert notices stale data

stem: A team wants a notification when the whole-table accuracy of the production model version falls below 0.85 in any window. The inference profile has both the prediction and the label column configured. Which source and filters feed the SQL alert?

choices.text: The drift metrics table, filtered to `column_name = 'prediction'`, alerting on `avg_delta`, because model quality is the change of the average prediction
The charts of the profile dashboard, because accuracy is calculated only when the dashboard is opened and is never stored in a table
The profile metrics table filtered to the column `label`, alerting on its `avg`, because the mean of a binary label equals the accuracy
The profile metrics table with `column_name = ':table'`, `slice_key IS NULL` and the production `model_id`, alerting on `accuracy_score`

stem: The validation set of a churn model is stored in `ml.churn.validation`. It has the same feature columns as the logged table of the endpoint, but no timestamp column, and two columns have other names and types. The team wants it as the baseline of an inference profile. What is the correct handling?

choices.text: Rename and cast the columns of the logged table to the validation set's names, because a baseline cannot be a view and cannot differ in types
Create a view that renames and casts the columns to the schema of the profiled table and use that view as the baseline; the timestamp column may be absent
Use it only for a snapshot profile, because inference profiles take their reference automatically from the first window of the primary table
Add a timestamp column holding the current time to the validation set, because a baseline table is not accepted without a timestamp column in it

stem: An engineer queries the drift metrics table of a time series profile and finds only rows with `drift_type = 'CONSECUTIVE'`. The team expected comparisons with the training distribution. What is missing?

choices.text: The granularity is too small, and baseline rows appear only for weekly or monthly granularities
The slicing expressions were not set, because baseline comparison is computed only for slices and not for the whole table
No baseline table was set in the profile configuration, and baseline drift is calculated only if a baseline table is provided
The profile has not been refreshed twice yet, because baseline rows are written only from the second refresh onward

stem: A retailer's traffic follows strong yearly seasonality. A time series profile with consecutive weekly drift raises false alarms every holiday week, while a baseline taken from last spring would also alarm. The team wants alerts only when holiday behavior itself changes. Which baseline fits?

choices.text: A baseline table holding the previous holiday period, so the current holiday window is compared with an acceptable seasonal distribution
A baseline table filled with synthetic uniform data, so that every real window differs from it by the same constant amount
A baseline table with the average of the entire previous year, because an average removes all seasonal influence
No baseline, and a consecutive drift alert with a higher threshold in December, which hides every other kind of change in that month as well as the holiday effect

stem: A retraining job overwrites the baseline table with the latest training data after each run, and the team notices that baseline drift stays near zero for months, even during a known upstream data change that the dashboards show clearly. What is the design flaw?

choices.text: Baseline drift is computed only at the first refresh and then frozen, so the later windows are never compared
The baseline moves with the data: a reference replaced by recent data is always the new normal, so it cannot expose changes since validation
The baseline table must be in a different catalog than the primary table, because otherwise both are read from the same cache
The baseline must have a timestamp column in its schema, because rows without timestamps are ignored by the drift calculation of the profile when it refreshes

stem: A nightly rewritten dimension table `ml.crm.customer_dim` has a snapshot profile. After a faulty load last month, the team wants drift information that shows when the distributions of the table move away from a version they consider healthy. What should they add?

choices.text: A time series profile on the load date, because snapshot profiles can never report drift of any kind against an earlier reference
A second snapshot profile on the same table, because one profile can compare only with rows added since its previous refresh and no more
Change data feed on the table, because drift metrics are written only for tables that have a change data feed enabled
A baseline table holding a copy of the table from when its distributions were acceptable, with the same schema

stem: An analyst runs `SELECT window.start, avg_delta FROM main.ml.tx_drift_metrics WHERE column_name = 'amount' AND drift_type = 'CONSECUTIVE' AND slice_key IS NULL` and sees `avg_delta = -4.2` for one window. What does this value mean?

choices.text: The average amount of that window is 4.2 percent of the average in the previous window
The average amount of that window is 4.2 above the average of the baseline table
The average is 4.2 below the previous window's, as delta is current minus comparison
The model's average prediction error fell by 4.2 relative to the previous window, as quality is also stored there

stem: Two versions of a regression model (ids `7` and `8`) served in parallel are logged into one inference table with a model version column configured as the model id column. The team wants the daily RMSE trend of each version for the whole table. Which query reads it from the profile metrics table?

choices.text: Query the profile metrics table with `column_name = ':table'`, `slice_key IS NULL` and `model_id IN (7, 8)`, ordered by `window.start`
Query the profile metrics table with `log_type = 'BASELINE'` and `column_name = 'prediction'`, grouped by version, for the daily error
Query the drift metrics table, filter `column_name = 'prediction'` and plot `avg_delta`, as the change of the mean prediction measures the error
Query the profile metrics table without slice filters, and average `root_mean_squared_error` over all rows, because every row is a separate model

stem: An inference profile for a binary classifier shows accuracy, precision, recall and F1 per window, but `log_loss` and `roc_auc_score` are NULL. The label and prediction columns are configured. What is missing?

choices.text: A baseline table, because the ranking and probability metrics are computed only for BASELINE rows
A weekly granularity, because threshold-free metrics are computed only over windows of seven days or more
A column with the predicted class probabilities, because log loss and ROC AUC require `prediction_proba_col`
A slicing expression on the label, because ROC AUC is produced only for sliced data

stem: Overall accuracy of a classifier has been flat for two months, but customer support reports poor results for one sales region. How can the team find out from the existing monitoring whether quality fell for that region?

choices.text: Add the region as the model id column so each region is monitored as a separate model, which also removes the model version from the profile
Add `slicing_exprs=["region"]` to the profile so that quality metrics are computed per region, and read the slices from the metric tables
Lower the granularity to one hour, because an hourly window shows regional differences that daily windows average out
Create a second inference profile on the same table filtered to the region, because a table may have several profiles with different filters

stem: The team's inference profile uses a constant string `prod` in the model id column for every request, whatever the served version. After version 3 replaced version 2, accuracy dips for a week and recovers. The team cannot tell whether version 3 caused the dip. What should they change?

choices.text: Delete the metric tables after every promotion so that the new version starts with a clean history
Lower the granularity to five minutes so that the day of the version switch is separated from the rest of the data
Replace the profile with a snapshot profile, which keeps one record for the table after each refresh and so shows the latest version only
Populate the model id column with the model version when unpacking the log, so that the profile computes metrics for each version separately

stem: A claims model predicts five damage classes. The class `structural` is rare and business critical. An analyst reads the `:table` rows of the profile metrics table and wants the weekly F1 of the `structural` class alone, not an average over classes. Which expression returns it?

choices.text: `f1_score.macro`, because the macro value is the F1 of the class with the lowest support in each window
`accuracy_score`, because with five classes the accuracy equals the F1 of the rarest class
`f1_score.one_vs_all['structural']`, which reads the F1 of that class from the per-class map of the struct
`f1_score.weighted`, because weighting by support puts the most weight on the rare class in each window

stem: The inference table logs a `sampling_fraction` below 1 for many rows because requests were down-sampled. A trend chart of daily request counts computed with `COUNT(*)` falls whenever the fraction is lowered although real traffic is steady. How should the volume trend be computed?

choices.text: Multiply the count by the number of served models, because each model logs an equal part of the requests
Weight each logged row by `1 / sampling_fraction`, for example `SUM(1 / sampling_fraction)`, to estimate the real number of requests
Keep `COUNT(*)` and accept that sampled logs cannot show volume, because down-sampling removes the information permanently and for every row
Replace the time window by a longer one, because the sampling fraction averages out over longer windows

stem: A fraud team wants to run a rewritten model on real production requests for two weeks while no caller ever receives its score. The production endpoint `fraud-prod` serves `current` at 100% of traffic. Which design implements this shadow evaluation?

choices.text: Enable scale to zero on a second served entity, so that the candidate wakes up only for a sample of the requests and its answers stay hidden from callers
Add the candidate as a second served entity at a 50% traffic percentage and discard its responses inside the calling service, so that half of all the live requests are scored by the new model
Register the candidate under the `champion` alias in Unity Catalog, so that the registry mirrors every production request into the new version for scoring
Keep `current` as the only model answering callers, and have the caller send a duplicate of each request to the candidate on its own endpoint, logging that output for offline comparison

stem: A `challenger` served entity receives 5% of the requests of an endpoint and was created with `scale_to_zero_enabled: true` to save cost. In the canary comparison its p99 latency shows irregular spikes, while `current` is steady, although both models run the same code path. What explains the spikes and what should be changed?

choices.text: The challenger's low request volume lets it idle and scale to zero, so some requests pay a cold start; turn off scale to zero for the canary so that the latency comparison is fair
The challenger's model signature differs from the current model's, which slows request parsing on that entity only; relog the model with the earlier signature
The update that added the challenger is still replacing the configuration, so requests alternate between old and new containers; wait for it to finish, then recompare
Route optimization applies only to the `current` entity, so the challenger uses the slower path; enable route optimization on the challenger served entity too

stem: An engineer submits a configuration update that moves `challenger` from 10% to 50%. While the endpoint shows Not ready (Updating), an alert shows that the error rate of the challenger's current 10% share is rising. The engineer wants to keep the 50% split from going live. What should be done?

choices.text: Delete the `challenger` served entity through its served-model route, which takes effect immediately and bypasses the configuration update in progress
Stop the endpoint, which discards the pending configuration and restores the 90/10 split when the endpoint is started again after the investigation
Cancel the in-progress update from the endpoint details page; the previous configuration keeps serving, and a new update can then set the split the team really wants
Send a second update that sets `current` back to 100%; the endpoint queues it and applies it ahead of the pending 50% change, so the split never goes live

stem: `recs-api` is a custom model endpoint created without route optimization. Traffic has grown, and the team wants the lower overhead latency of route optimization, with a rollback path that leaves the old service untouched. Which plan fits?

choices.text: Create a new route-optimized endpoint for the same model version, validate it with OAuth test calls to its own URL, move clients over, and keep the old endpoint until confidence is high
Edit the existing endpoint's configuration to turn on route optimization, and roll back by editing it off again if the latency does not improve for the clients
Add a route-optimized served entity to the existing endpoint at 100% traffic and set the old entity to 0%, which keeps the previous version available for a quick rollback later
Create the route-optimized endpoint and keep clients on personal access tokens, since only the endpoint URL changes and authentication stays as it was before

stem: An endpoint serves `current` at 95% and `challenger` at 5%. Peak load is 200 requests per second and the model needs about 0.1 s per request. Both entities were created with the same large compute scale-out. Which configuration follows Databricks sizing guidance better?

choices.text: Give every served entity the concurrency for the full endpoint peak, because the platform may route any request to any entity and each entity must be able to take all of the load alone
Give the challenger the largest scale-out available, because a new model version is slower on its first requests and needs the extra capacity until it warms up
Use one scale-out value for both entities that is derived from the average of their sizes, so that comparisons of their latency are not distorted by compute differences
Size each served entity from its own share: concurrency is roughly queries per second times execution time, so the challenger needs about 5% of the peak load's concurrency and `current` about 95%

stem: A release plan for a custom model endpoint has three edits: add `challenger` as a served entity, set the split to 90/10, and enlarge the compute size of `current`. The engineer plans to submit them as three consecutive API calls. What is the problem and the better approach?

choices.text: Each call must go to a different endpoint, because a single endpoint accepts exactly one changed property per update to keep rollbacks atomic
Only one update can run at a time and each is billed for both configurations while it runs; submit a single configuration update that contains all three changes together
Traffic split changes need no configuration update, so only the first and third edits are sent as updates and the split is applied later as a request parameter by clients
There is no problem, because the platform merges queued updates for the same endpoint into a single rebuild before the new configuration is provisioned

stem: A challenger model was trained on restricted data, and only the data science group may send requests to it. All application services may query the current model. How should the challenger be exposed for validation?

choices.text: Deploy it on its own endpoint and grant CAN_QUERY on that endpoint only to the data science group, because permissions are assigned per endpoint, not per served entity
Alias the challenger version as `challenger` and grant the alias to the group; applications calling the endpoint then can never be routed to it by the traffic split
Serve it from the production endpoint and restrict EXECUTE on the model in Unity Catalog to the data science group, so other callers are rejected when the split picks it
Add it to the production endpoint as a served entity with a small traffic percentage and set a separate query permission on that served entity for the data science group

stem: A custom pyfunc model is registered in Unity Catalog. It works in a notebook but fails when served: ``` def predict(self, context, model_input): w = torch.load("/Volumes/ml/prod/weights/model.pt") return score(w, model_input) ``` Which change makes the file available at serving time?

choices.text: Copy the file to a DBFS root folder and read it from a `/dbfs/...` path inside `predict`, since serving containers share the cluster's mounted file systems
Log the model with `artifacts={"weights": "/Volumes/ml/prod/weights/model.pt"}` and load the file in `load_context` through `context.artifacts["weights"]`
Attach an instance profile to the endpoint so that it can read the volume path directly from cloud storage at request time, then keep the code unchanged
Grant the endpoint's service principal READ VOLUME on the volume and keep the path in the code, because the endpoint mounts Unity Catalog volumes while it serves

stem: A custom pyfunc loads a large embedding file and builds a tokenizer inside `predict` on every call. After deployment, median latency is far above what the same model reaches in a notebook loop. How should the class be restructured?

choices.text: Enable scale to zero so that idle replicas release memory between requests and each new request loads the objects into a freshly started container
Cache the loaded objects in a module-level global of the notebook that logged the model, so every served replica reuses the same in-memory copy
Raise the endpoint's request timeout so slow loads in `predict` finish successfully, and size the served entity up to hide the repeated cost
Build the tokenizer and read the embedding file once in `load_context`, store them on `self`, and keep only the per-request logic in `predict`

stem: A pyfunc model is logged from a Databricks Runtime ML cluster without `pip_requirements`. Registration in Unity Catalog works, but every endpoint build fails. The model's `conda.yaml` lists `mlflow-skinny`. What is the fix?

choices.text: Remove the model signature and input example, because they pull the skinny package into the environment file during logging
Add `mlflow-skinny` to `extra_pip_requirements` with an exact version pin, which makes the container builder accept the skinny package as the MLflow dependency
Log a new model version with `pip_requirements` naming `mlflow==<version>` (the full package) and the other libraries it needs, then serve that version
Move the endpoint to a GPU workload type, whose base image ships the full MLflow package and ignores the model's recorded environment

stem: A pyfunc preprocessing module is published as an internal wheel on the company's Artifactory mirror. Policy forbids public internet access from endpoints, and workspace admins have set Artifactory as the workspace default package repository. What is the simplest correct way to include the library?

choices.text: Run `%pip install` of the wheel in the notebook that logs the model; Model Serving copies the installed packages of the cluster into the container
Set a `PIP_INDEX_URL` environment variable on the served entity, so that the container downloads the wheel from the mirror each time a request arrives
List the library in the model's pip requirements, so that Model Serving installs it from the workspace default package repository while building the container
Package the wheel in a Unity Catalog volume and list the volume path in `extra_pip_requirements`, since serving never uses a configured package mirror

stem: A pyfunc loads a tokenizer in `load_context`: ``` self.tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("acme/ner-tokenizer") ``` Network policies now block outbound internet access from endpoints, and new endpoint versions fail while loading the model. What is the correct redesign?

choices.text: Move the download into `predict` and wrap it in a retry, so that blocked calls are retried until the network policy admits the connection
Download the tokenizer files at logging time, pass the directory in `artifacts`, and load it from `context.artifacts` with `local_files_only=True`
Store the hub access token in a plain text environment variable of the served entity, so the container is authorized to pass the outbound restriction
Keep the download in `load_context` and raise the endpoint's request timeout, because the model load then has more time to reach the public hub

stem: A team registers a pyfunc to Unity Catalog: ``` mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc") mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(name="m", python_model=M(), registered_model_name="ml.prod.scorer") ``` The call fails with an error saying the model has no signature metadata. What resolves it?

choices.text: Register under a two-level name such as `prod.scorer`, because three-level names are only accepted by the legacy workspace model registry
Request the EXECUTE privilege on the schema for the logging identity, since the registration fails until the identity may run models in that schema
Switch the registry URI to the workspace model registry, because pyfunc models without a signature are accepted only there and not in Unity Catalog
Pass a model signature (for example `infer_signature(sample_input, sample_output)`) when logging, because Unity Catalog requires input and output schemas

stem: Before creating an endpoint for a new pyfunc version, the team wants to detect missing packages and environment errors without deploying anything. Which check matches Databricks guidance?

choices.text: Run `mlflow.models.predict` with the model URI and a sample input, which executes the model in an environment rebuilt from its recorded requirements
Compare the model's `requirements.txt` with `pip freeze` output of the logging cluster by eye, since matching version numbers prove that deployment will succeed
Create the production endpoint with the new version at 100% traffic and read the build logs, since only a real deployment tests the serving container
Call `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model` in the logging notebook and invoke `predict`; the notebook has the same packages, so passing proves the container will build

stem: A pyfunc reads features by position, `model_input.iloc[:, 0]` for age and `iloc[:, 1]` for income. Callers send: ``` {"dataframe_records": [{"income": 52000, "age": 34}]} ``` Predictions in production differ from the notebook. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Wrap the same body in the `inputs` key, because that key makes the endpoint apply the model signature's column order to dictionary rows
Send `dataframe_split` with an explicit `columns` list and have the model select columns by name, because the records format does not guarantee column order
Switch the request to the `instances` key, which Databricks documents as the preferred format for tabular models with named columns
Keep the records format but sort the keys alphabetically in the client, since Databricks reads the keys in sorted order when it builds the DataFrame

stem: A service principal calls a route-optimized endpoint at its dedicated URL with an OAuth token minted using `grant_type=client_credentials&scope=all-apis`. Every call returns 401 with the message that authorization details are missing. What must change?

choices.text: Request the token with `authorization_details` naming the endpoint ID and the `query_inference_endpoint` action, since a plain `all-apis` token is not scoped to it
Change the token request scope to `serving-endpoints`, because the token endpoint rejects `all-apis` for route-optimized URLs and requires an endpoint scope
Replace the OAuth token with a personal access token of a workspace admin, since the dedicated route accepts any token that carries the all-apis scope
Send the request to the workspace invocations URL instead, because endpoints created recently accept only workspace URLs and tokens without detail claims

stem: An external Python service must query a newly created route-optimized endpoint with as little custom auth code as possible. A service principal with CAN_QUERY exists. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Send requests to the workspace invocations URL with the service principal's OAuth token, since the same URL serves every endpoint created after the change
Call `ai_query` from a SQL warehouse for each request and return the result to the service, since the function takes care of the URL and the token
Use a `WorkspaceClient` configured with a personal access token and call `serving_endpoints.query`, because the SDK handles route optimization for personal tokens
Build a Databricks SDK `WorkspaceClient` from the host and the service principal's client ID and secret, then call `serving_endpoints_data_plane.query` with the endpoint name

stem: A Python job in a Databricks notebook and a Java web service must both query the same custom model endpoint (not route optimized). Which pairing of methods is right?

choices.text: The notebook posts raw REST requests only, because the Deployments SDK is limited to external models, and the Java service uses the SDK's Java package
Both use `ai_query`, because it is the documented method for application calls to custom model endpoints and accepts the same JSON bodies
The notebook uses the Deployments SDK client's `predict`, and the Java service posts JSON to `/serving-endpoints/<name>/invocations` with an M2M OAuth token
The Java service calls `mlflow.deployments` through a Python subprocess, since REST access to custom model endpoints is limited to code running inside Databricks notebooks

stem: A pyfunc receives requests with missing columns and currently raises `ValueError`; clients see an unexpected-error response and the on-call rota is paged on server-error rates. How should the model code be changed so that malformed client input does not look like a platform fault?

choices.text: Disable the model signature on the endpoint, because signature validation is what turns malformed requests into server errors on the platform
Validate the input in `predict` and raise `MlflowException` with a clear message, since those errors map to 4xx and 5xx is reserved for faults on the Databricks side
Catch every exception in `predict` and return an empty prediction list with a 200 status, which keeps the error rate low and lets callers detect any missing output themselves
Wrap the request body in an `inputs` key on the client, since the key makes the endpoint convert all model exceptions into client errors

stem: Clients of a standard (not route-optimized) endpoint get HTTP 429 with the message `Exceeded max number of parallel requests` while the served entity still shows spare provisioned concurrency. Which remedy does Databricks recommend first?

choices.text: Switch the request body from `dataframe_split` to `dataframe_records`, because the records format sends fewer parallel connections per client
Turn on scale to zero for the served entity so that idle capacity is released and the workspace limit is shared among fewer replicas
Raise the provisioned concurrency of the served entity, which lifts the workspace-wide limit on parallel requests that clients may send at once
Create a route-optimized endpoint, where this workspace-level parallel request limit does not apply, and move the clients to it

stem: A service principal gets `403 Permission denied` from a route-optimized endpoint although its token was minted with `authorization_details`. The principal is a workspace member. What should be checked?

choices.text: Whether the service principal has CAN_QUERY on the endpoint and whether the action in the token's `authorization_details` matches its granted permission
Whether the service principal holds EXECUTE on the served Unity Catalog model, because every caller is checked against model privileges at each single request
Whether the token was issued by a personal access token exchange, because route-optimized endpoints accept only tokens exchanged from user logins
Whether the service principal is a workspace admin, because only admins may query route-optimized endpoints at their dedicated URLs with OAuth

stem: A deployment script fails to create the endpoint: ``` client = mlflow.deployments.get_deploy_client("databricks") client.create_endpoint(name="databricks-churn-v2", config={"served_entities": [{ "entity_name": "ml.prod.churn", "entity_version": "4", "workload_size": "Small", "scale_to_zero_enabled": False}]}) ``` Model, version and permissions are correct. What is wrong?

choices.text: The `entity_name` must be given as a `models:/` URI for Unity Catalog models, so the three-level name is not resolved by `create_endpoint`
The `workload_size` must be omitted when `scale_to_zero_enabled` is `False`, because compute is then sized by autoscaling alone
The endpoint name starts with `databricks-`, a prefix reserved for preconfigured endpoints; the name must change
The client must be created with `get_deploy_client("databricks-uc")`, because the plain `databricks` target only serves workspace registry models

stem: A CI job running as a service principal creates an endpoint for `ml.prod.scorer`. The principal is a workspace member with the workspace-access entitlement, but creation fails with `PERMISSION_DENIED`. Which grants should be added to the principal?

choices.text: `CAN_MANAGE` on the workspace's Serving UI and `ALL PRIVILEGES` on the metastore, because endpoint creation checks account-level administration rights
`READ VOLUME` on every volume the model was trained from and `CREATE MODEL` on the schema, because the endpoint copies the training files into the container
`USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema and `EXECUTE` on the model, which are validated at endpoint creation or update for the recorded creator
`SELECT` on the tables that were used to train the model and `MODIFY` on the model's schema, because serving replays the training data when the endpoint starts

stem: An endpoint created through the SDK stays not ready, and its event log shows that the container image was built. After startup, requests fail with `An error occurred while loading the model. No module named 'acme_prep'`, where `acme_prep` is an internal wheel the model imports. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Log a new model version that declares the wheel as a dependency (for example in `extra_pip_requirements`) and update the endpoint to it, which triggers a new build
Increase the served entity's workload size, since a larger container has more preinstalled libraries and may include internal packages
Wait for the build to finish, because Databricks asks you to contact support only if the container build shows no result after about ten minutes of waiting
Install the wheel with `%pip` on the cluster that runs the deployment script and restart the endpoint, so the loaded model finds the package

stem: A release pipeline updates an endpoint to model version 7 with a configuration call that returns successfully and then marks the deployment finished. An hour later monitoring still shows version 6 answers and the endpoint status reads Ready (Update failed). What does this mean and how should the pipeline be changed?

choices.text: The endpoint accepted version 7 and is only slow to refresh its status label; the pipeline should ignore this status and compare model outputs instead
The endpoint is down for all requests until the update is repeated; the pipeline should call the update again immediately to restore service
Version 7 serves at a reduced rate beside version 6 because the update succeeded partially; the pipeline should wait until the split balances itself
The update failed and version 6 kept serving; the pipeline should poll the endpoint state until the update ends, fail the release on a failed update, and read the events and logs

stem: A pyfunc calls a partner API with the key from `os.environ["PARTNER_API_KEY"]`. The team deploys it with the SDK and must keep the key out of the model artifact and the endpoint configuration text. What is the right setup?

choices.text: Place the key in a text file in a volume and pass that file in `artifacts`, since artifacts are encrypted and hidden from endpoint readers
Keep the key in a Databricks secret scope and set the served entity's environment variable to `{{secrets/partner/api_key}}`; the endpoint creator needs READ on the secret
Set the environment variable to the key as plain text in the served entity, since endpoint configurations are visible only to the endpoint creator
Log the key as an MLflow parameter of the run and read it from `context.model_config` at request time, so it travels with the registered model version everywhere

stem: A team deploys new versions of a custom pyfunc model often. Deployments wait a long time for container image builds, some fail on dependency resolution, and the serving environment sometimes differs from the notebook used for training. Which option addresses all three, and what does it cost?

choices.text: Set scale to zero on the served entity so that the container image is cached between versions, at the price of cold starts on the first request
Pin every dependency to the latest release in `pip_requirements`, which removes dependency resolution from the build, at the price of frequent relogging
Use express deployments: register the custom model to Unity Catalog from a serverless notebook so the environment is packaged then, and accept a longer registration step
Enable route optimization on the existing endpoint, which skips the image build and gives the endpoint the notebook's environment, at the price of OAuth-only access for clients

stem: After a release, a post-processing step in a pyfunc triples the model execution time per request. Traffic is unchanged, and clients now receive 429 with `Too many concurrent requests. Consider increasing the provisioned concurrency of the served entity`. What is the right remedy?

choices.text: Switch the request format to `dataframe_records` so that rows are scored in parallel, which divides the execution time by the number of rows
Raise the served entity's scale-out (or autoscaling maximum) to about three times the earlier concurrency, since required concurrency is roughly QPS times execution time
Enable scale to zero on the served entity, so that the platform keeps fewer idle slots and the pool of slots grows only when 429 errors appear in the client logs
Increase the client request timeout above the model execution time, since a longer wait lets concurrency rise by itself without config changes

stem: A multitask Lakeflow job runs `train`, then `validate`, then `deploy`. The validation task must evaluate exactly the model version that this run's training task registered, even when two runs execute at the same time. How should the version reach the validation task?

choices.text: The training task publishes the model URI as a task value, and the validation task reads it from the upstream task
The training task writes the model URI to a file under `/tmp`, and the validation task reads that file from its own compute
The validation task loads `models:/prod.ml.churn@champion`, because the alias always names the newest candidate version
The validation task calls `get_latest_versions` on the model name, because the highest version number is always the current run's

stem: A deployment task gives the Champion alias to every model version that the validation task marked as Challenger, with no further step. After two weeks, a version with a lower AUC than its predecessor is serving production. What is missing from the deployment pipeline in the recommended Databricks workflow?

choices.text: A second validation task that repeats the same format and metadata checks directly before the alias is moved
A Model Serving endpoint with a traffic split, because an alias update is only allowed behind a served endpoint
A retraining step that loops until the new version shows a higher AUC than the current Champion version
A comparison of the Challenger with the existing Champion on held-out data, and an alias update only when it wins

stem: A model version fails the model validation task because its accuracy on one customer segment is below the agreed threshold. What should the validation pipeline do under the recommended Databricks workflow?

choices.text: Assign the Challenger alias anyway, because the deployment step compares it with the Champion afterwards
Delete the failing version and start training again automatically until a version passes the checks
Move the Champion alias to an older version so that production serves a model that is known to pass
Record the failure on the model version, withhold the Challenger alias, end the run and notify the owners

stem: A team ships its first churn model. The deployment pipeline compares the Challenger with the Champion, but no version holds the Champion alias yet, so the comparison task fails. What does the recommended Databricks workflow suggest?

choices.text: Assign Champion to the oldest version of the registered model so that the comparison has a model to read
Compare the Challenger with a business heuristic or another agreed threshold used as the baseline
Skip both the validation task and the comparison for the first release, because there is no model to compare with
Hold the release until a second model version exists, so that the pipeline always has two models to compare

stem: During development, data scientists chose AUC and a custom cost-weighted error as the evaluation metrics. The weekly training pipeline in production now has to evaluate each new model. What does the recommended Databricks workflow specify for the evaluation step?

choices.text: It scores the training rows themselves, so that no other production data is read outside the training task
It uses new metrics chosen by the ML engineers, because data scientists have no part in the production pipeline
It tests on held-out production data with the metrics from development and logs them to the production tracking server
It computes accuracy only, because custom metric code is not allowed in production pipelines on Databricks

stem: A team promotes only the model artifact (deploy models). After months, the production inference notebook no longer matches the feature engineering code used in development, and predictions are skewed. Which statement gives the structural cause and the recommended remedy?

choices.text: Only the artifact is promoted, so supporting code goes separately; adopt deploy code so all pipelines pass the same tests
Aliases do not work with batch inference, so the inference job should load models by hard-coded version numbers
Unity Catalog models cannot store feature dependencies, so the team must export the feature code into every model
The model should be retrained in production every day, because stale models cause feature code to drift

stem: Security policy blocks the development workspace from reading production data. A team that promotes only trained models (deploy models) therefore trains on synthetic samples in development. Which limitation of the pattern does this show, and what does Databricks recommend in most situations?

choices.text: Models cannot be registered in Unity Catalog from development, so the team has to register them from production
Synthetic samples are not allowed in any pattern, so Databricks recommends copying production data into development
The pattern forbids Git, so Databricks recommends moving exported notebooks by hand between the workspaces
The pattern may not be viable without production data in development, so Databricks recommends promoting code

stem: An auditor asks which parameters, input data and code produced version 12 of a registered model. Which Databricks capability records that link at training time?

choices.text: A Model Serving endpoint, which lists the served versions and the routing percentages
An MLflow run that logs parameters, metrics, the model and a link to the data and code
The Champion alias on the registered model, which names the version that serves production
A Lakeflow Jobs schedule, which stores the cron expression and the next trigger time

stem: A bank needs one governed place that holds model versions across development, staging and production, with per-environment permissions, version history and a marker for the version in use. Which feature mapping fits?

choices.text: Models in Unity Catalog, a catalog per environment, and aliases such as Champion
One feature table per environment, with the model weights stored as a column of the table
Git branches named dev, staging and release, with a tag on each commit that trained a model
One MLflow experiment per environment, with experiment permissions and run tags marking the stage of each run

stem: An ML engineer wants training, validation and deployment to run in order, with the next step skipped and the owners notified if a step fails. Which feature maps to this lifecycle activity?

choices.text: A Unity Catalog volume that stores the intermediate artifacts of each task
An MLflow experiment with autologging enabled for the training library
A multitask Lakeflow job with task dependencies and failure notifications
A Model Serving endpoint with several served models and a traffic split

stem: A regulator requires that a person approves each new Champion, although the validation and deployment tasks are automated. Which feature of the Databricks workflow supports such a manual approval step?

choices.text: An MLflow autologging setting that pauses the training run until a reviewer opens the experiment page
Job notifications or CI/CD callbacks from the deployment pipeline, which hold the alias update for the approver
A Unity Catalog tag on the model version that the deployment task sets to approved before the alias moves
A Model Serving traffic split of 0 percent for the Challenger, which the endpoint owner raises after reviewing it

stem: A recommendation model was trained with features from Unity Catalog feature tables. Client applications should send only the user ID to the endpoint, and the endpoint should add the stored features. What must the training pipeline do?

choices.text: Copy the feature values into the request payload from a nightly export of the feature tables, refreshed every hour
Write a custom model that reads the offline feature table with Spark inside its predict function
Log the model with the Feature Engineering client and the training set, so lookups are packaged
Log the model with a plain flavor log function and join the features in the client application

stem: Before the alias update, the team wants an offline comparison of a Challenger and the Champion on a held-out dataset, with both results kept for later audit. Which feature carries this lifecycle activity?

choices.text: Evaluating both versions in the deployment pipeline and tracking the results with the MLflow Tracking server
Unity Catalog lineage, which computes and stores the metrics of every version that reads a table
A Model Serving endpoint that sends half of the traffic to each model, compared through the request logs
A Lakeflow Jobs schedule, which keeps the metric values of earlier runs as run parameters

stem: A team wants code to move between stages by review: dev branch, main branch, release branch, with notebooks and modules synchronized to each workspace. Which feature carries this lifecycle activity?

choices.text: Notebook exports saved to a shared workspace folder, which colleagues import
MLflow code snapshots stored with each run, which are copied between workspaces
Unity Catalog volumes holding zip files of the code, mounted in each environment
Databricks Git folders connected to the project's Git repository and its branches

stem: An engineer wants to run pytest interactively on Spark-based feature functions in the workspace. The web terminal opens quickly. Why does Databricks recommend writing and running the unit tests in a notebook instead?

choices.text: The web terminal has limits, such as no support for Spark, while a notebook runs on compute with a Spark session
Pytest refuses to start in any shell, so a notebook is the only tool that can import the test modules
The web terminal deletes installed packages after every single command, so pytest would be installed again every time
Only notebooks can read files in a Git folder, because the terminal has no access to repository files

stem: A notebook job calls `pytest.main` every night and the task fails on its assertion. The engineer needs the list of individual tests that failed. Where does Databricks say the results of the unit test run can be viewed?

choices.text: In the Git folder, where pytest writes a results file into the repository after each run
In the Unity Catalog audit log, which stores the text output of each notebook cell
In the MLflow experiment of the job, where every test is logged as a metric without any extra code
In the cluster's driver logs, or at the log delivery location that is set for the cluster

stem: A unit test for a function that deduplicates transactions reads `prod.ml.transactions` and runs the function that deletes duplicate rows in place. A colleague objects. What is the right design?

choices.text: Point the test at a limited sample of production rows and delete duplicates only inside that sample of rows
Build a small DataFrame of fake rows that resembles production data and run the function
Run the test only at night, when fewer users query the production table
Grant the test account read-only rights and keep the production table as the input

stem: A notebook job runs the lines below. The job task always shows success, even when a test fails. ``` import pytest pytest.main([".", "-v", "-p", "no:cacheprovider"]) ``` What is the fix?

choices.text: Add the `-x` flag so that pytest stops at the first failure and the stop is reported as the status
Install pytest with `%pip` in the same cell, so that failures stop being swallowed
Keep the return value of `pytest.main` and assert it equals 0, so a failure fails the cell
Wrap the call in try/except and print any exception, so that failures show up in the cell output

stem: A new test file called `checks_features.py` contains functions named `check_age_bucket` and `check_null_rate`. Running `pytest .` in the notebook reports that no tests were run. What is the cause?

choices.text: Pytest collects `test_*.py` or `*_test.py` files and `test_*` functions, so neither name matches
Pytest only runs tests that are stored inside notebooks, so the file must be converted to a notebook first
Pytest needs a Spark session fixture before it can collect any test from a file
Pytest skips files that import from other modules in the same Git folder

stem: A test notebook runs pytest from a Git folder on a read-only file system, where writing `.pyc` files and a pytest cache folder fails. Which settings does the Databricks example use to avoid this?

choices.text: `spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.ignoreCorruptFiles", "true")` set before the call to pytest
`sys.dont_write_bytecode = True` and the `-p no:cacheprovider` argument in the `pytest.main` call
`pytest.main([".", "-q"])` alone, because pytest never writes files unless an extra plugin is installed
`%sh rm -rf .pytest_cache` as the last cell, so that the folders only exist while the run is in progress

stem: Unit tests are started by hand from a notebook, and changes sometimes reach the main branch without being tested. The team wants the same tests to run automatically whenever code changes. What does Databricks suggest?

choices.text: Attach the tests to the Model Serving endpoint, so that they run when each request arrives
Ask every developer to run the notebook before merging and to write the result in the pull request
Set up a CI/CD system such as GitHub Actions that runs the unit tests whenever the code changes
Convert the tests into a scheduled SQL alert that sends an email when a run fails at night

stem: A reviewer wants to know where the final unit and integration tests run in the deploy code pattern, compared with the deploy models pattern. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: Deploy code runs the final tests in development; deploy models runs them in staging
Deploy code runs the final tests in production; deploy models runs them in staging
Both patterns run the final tests in development and use staging only for the load test
Deploy code runs the final tests in staging; deploy models runs them in development

stem: A model team reviews three automated checks. One calls a feature function on a three-row DataFrame and asserts the result. One triggers the feature, training and inference pipelines in sequence against the staging catalog. One sends a few requests to a temporary staging endpoint. Which classification is right?

choices.text: The first is a unit test, and the second and third are integration tests
All three are integration tests, because each runs in the staging workspace
The first and third are unit tests, because they use test data, and the second is a system test
The first and second are unit tests, because they run on small data, and the third is a load test

stem: An integration test fails in a staging CI run. The data scientist cannot reproduce the failure in development, because the tables that show it exist only in the staging catalog. What does Databricks guidance say about access?

choices.text: Give development write access to the production catalog, because production holds the same tables as staging
Switch off the staging catalog and run all integration tests in development, where debugging is simpler
Copy the whole staging catalog into development after every run, and delete the staging tables once the copy exists
Give development access to the staging catalog for debugging, and keep running the integration tests in staging

stem: Integration tests pass in staging, but the first production run fails because the staging job used a different library set and cluster settings than the production job. What does Databricks guidance say about the staging environment?

choices.text: It should be identical to production including the full data volume, whatever the time and cost
It should be as small as possible, because integration tests check logic and never configuration
It should match production as closely as is reasonable, trading some fidelity for speed or cost where needed
It only has to match production in catalog names, because compute and libraries do not affect pipeline results

stem: In the production stage the training pipeline registered a new version, and the team argues that the staging integration tests already proved quality, so the pipeline may assign Challenger directly. Which check is still needed?

choices.text: A second round of unit tests of the feature functions, run on production data
The production validation task, with format, metadata, slice and compliance checks on the new version
A manual rerun of the staging integration tests against the production catalog before each retraining
Nothing, since training code that passed in staging produces equivalent models in production

stem: The unit tests of the feature function and of the training function both pass. In staging, the training task fails because the feature pipeline writes the column `cust_id` while the training pipeline reads `customer_id`. Which kind of test is meant to catch this, and where does it run?

choices.text: A unit test of the feature function, run again in development on a larger sample of rows
A unit test of the training function, run in the production workspace on the live feature tables
An integration test that runs the feature and the training pipelines together, run in staging by CI
A load test of the serving endpoint, run in staging with the full production request volume

stem: Integration tests on a pull request fail in the inference stage. The CI system currently only turns its status red. What should the CI/CD system also do, according to Databricks guidance, before the code can reach the main branch?

choices.text: Notify the users and post the results on the pull request, and merge only after the tests pass
Rerun only the unit tests until the status turns green, then merge the change automatically
Delete the pull request branch and ask the author to create the change again from the main branch
Merge the change anyway and open a ticket, because inference failures are repaired after release

stem: A data profile on an inference table refreshes every night and writes its drift metrics table each time, whether or not anything drifted. A table update trigger on that table starts the retraining job, and now a model is trained and registered every night, mostly on unchanged data. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Point the trigger at the profile metrics table instead, because that table receives new rows only in windows where some feature has drifted
Keep the trigger; a first task counts features above the baseline drift limit as a task value, and an If/else task trains only when the count is at least 1
Replace the trigger by a weekly cron schedule, because a table update trigger always starts a run and offers no check of the table contents
Raise the minimum time between triggers to seven days, so that the trigger itself inspects the table and skips the run when no drift is found

stem: In a retraining job, a `train` notebook task registers a new model version and a downstream `validate` task must evaluate exactly that version. Today `validate` loads the highest version number of the model from the registry. Twice, two overlapping job runs made `validate` test a version that the other run had trained. How should the version reach the validation task?

choices.text: Let `train` write the version number to a file on its driver's local disk and let `validate` read that file
Define a job parameter for the version number and let the scheduler fill it in before the run starts
Add a fixed sleep at the start of `validate`, so that the other run has finished registering its own version before the highest one is read
Let `train` set a task value `model_version` with `dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set` and give `validate` the reference `{{tasks.train.values.model_version}}`

stem: A drift alert fires and starts the retraining job. The investigation shows that an upstream pipeline change set a feature to null for 40% of rows (`percent_null_delta` jumped), and the real customer behavior did not change. Retraining on the new data would bake the defect into the model. How should the automated pipeline be designed?

choices.text: Retrain immediately on the newest data so that the new model learns the missing values, and lower the alert threshold to catch such cases earlier
Add a data quality gate before training that checks null rates and schema against expectations and stops the run, then route the incident to the data owner
Retrain twice, on the old and on the new data, and promote whichever model has the higher training accuracy, to avoid a decision about the data
Disable drift alerts for that feature permanently, because a feature that can be corrupted upstream is not reliable enough to monitor

stem: A fraud model receives its true labels about 45 days after scoring. A team wants automated retraining but worries that waiting for accuracy to drop means 45 days of damage. Feature drift against the training baseline is available daily. Which trigger design best balances speed and reliability?

choices.text: Retrain only when labelled accuracy falls below the target, and never use drift, because drift can occur while the model stays accurate
Retrain on every drift alert and ignore labels, since waiting for performance numbers would only delay each model update further
Use feature drift as an early signal that starts a candidate run, and let labelled performance and a champion comparison confirm the promotion
Retrain every night on a rolling window, because a schedule is the only trigger type that does not depend on delayed labels

stem: A price-sensitivity model is retrained six weeks after a regulatory change that altered customer behavior abruptly and permanently on 1 September. The training table holds three years of history. Which training window gives the retrained model the best chance to match current behavior?

choices.text: The post-change days plus older data that is down-weighted or marked with a regime flag, with a time-ordered holdout taken after the change
All three years with equal weight, because more rows always lower the variance and the regulatory change affects only one date in the whole history
Only the six weeks since the change, with the older rows deleted for good, so that the model sees no stale behavior at all
A random sample over the three years, because random sampling removes the effect of the date on which the change happened

stem: A lending model is retrained monthly on all applications with a known repayment outcome. Only approved applicants have outcomes, because rejected applicants never received a loan. Each retrain makes the model more confident about the kind of applicant it already approves, and drift alerts on the application data stay quiet. What is the underlying problem and the mitigation?

choices.text: The model suffers from concept drift in every single month, so the retraining schedule should move from monthly to weekly or to even shorter intervals
The PSI limit is too wide to see the problem, so it should be lowered until an alert fires after each retrain
Approved applicants are too few for training, so the approved rows should be oversampled until the classes balance
The labels exist only for cases the model approved, which biases the data; approve a small random share for exploration or use reject inference

stem: A scheduled retraining job trains a model and registers it in Unity Catalog as `prod.ml.churn`. Batch scoring and a serving endpoint load `models:/prod.ml.churn@Champion`. The team wants retraining to be fully automatic, but a new version must not reach production unless it beats the current model. Which last stage of the job fits?

choices.text: Overwrite the files of the champion version in the registry with the new model weights so that the alias keeps its target
Write the new model to a volume as a pickle file and ask a reviewer to copy it over the champion by hand
Register the version, give it a Challenger alias, evaluate it against the champion, and move Champion to it only if the gate passes
Register the new version and set the Champion alias to it at once, then run the evaluation in a later job and roll back by deleting the version

stem: The nightly retraining job produces a challenger. The registry stores metrics from the time each version was trained, and the champion's stored AUC is 0.91 from three months ago. The challenger scores 0.89 on today's holdout. An engineer suggests promoting only if the challenger's number beats the stored one. What is the flaw, and what should the job do?

choices.text: The comparison is fine; a lower number means the challenger is worse, so the job should keep the champion and stop
Both models should be scored on the same current holdout, including the champion, because the stored number came from older data and a different split
The challenger should be compared by its training loss, since loss does not depend on which holdout was used for the comparison
The stored metric is a training-time value; the challenger should be compared on test data from the training pipeline only, never on newer data

stem: A pricing model uses the predicted default probability directly in a formula (expected loss = probability x exposure). Retraining yields two candidates: model X has the higher AUC, model Y has the lower log loss and a reliability curve close to the diagonal. Which should the pipeline prefer, and why?

choices.text: Model X, because AUC is threshold independent and therefore the only metric that matters for any model that outputs a probability
Model X, because a higher AUC guarantees that its probabilities are better calibrated, so log loss and the reliability curve would only repeat the same information
Model Y, because log loss is always lower for the simpler model, so lower log loss proves that Y generalizes better than X
Model Y, because the formula needs probabilities matching observed frequencies, which log loss and calibration measure and AUC does not

stem: A fraud model sees 0.4% positive transactions. Automated retraining picks the challenger with the highest validation accuracy, and last month's pick missed most fraud while showing 99.6% accuracy. Fraud ops can review a fixed number of alerts per day. Which selection metric should the pipeline use?

choices.text: Precision-recall AUC, or recall at the precision the review capacity allows, on a holdout
Mean squared error of the hard 0/1 predictions, because it penalizes each wrong decision equally
ROC AUC on the training set, because it is not affected by the share of positive examples
Validation accuracy again, but averaged over five random seeds and several cross-validation folds to make the comparison more stable

stem: A weekly retraining job promotes the challenger whenever its validation AUC exceeds the champion's. Over several weeks the champion alias flips back and forth between nearly identical models, which causes churn in downstream approvals. Differences are around 0.001 AUC. How should the promotion rule change?

choices.text: Promote only if the improvement exceeds a minimum margin and a bootstrap interval of the difference on the holdout excludes zero
Remove the gate and let each new model become the champion automatically, because newer models always reflect the latest data better and need no check
Retrain more often, so that more candidates are compared and the best of many replaces the champion
Compare on the training set instead, where the difference between candidates is larger and easier to detect

stem: A retraining job runs a hyperparameter search and then selects the best run. The final reported performance in production is regularly lower than the logged value. The selection code is: runs = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=[exp_id], order_by=["metrics.test_auc DESC"], max_results=1) best = runs.iloc[0]["run_id"] What is the main problem with this approach?

choices.text: The job should select by the training AUC instead, since the test set is not available to the registry
It orders by the metric ascending, so the job selects the worst run of the whole experiment and the result is lower in production than logged
`search_runs` reads only the first run of an experiment, so the best run is never part of the result
Choosing by test metric makes the test set part of model choice and biases it; select on validation and score the test set once

stem: The automated promotion gate must accept a challenger only if the primary metric improves, p95 scoring latency stays under the application limit, and the input and output signature stays compatible with callers of the champion. Which design is best?

choices.text: Promote on the primary metric alone and ask the application team to report latency and signature problems after the release
Combine the three values into one weighted score and promote above a threshold, so that a very good metric can offset a failed latency limit
Log the metrics and the signature check as outputs of an evaluation task, and let an If/else gate move the Champion alias only when all conditions pass
Move the Champion alias first and run the checks afterwards, so that a failing check triggers a rollback by moving the alias back

stem: A demand model is retrained weekly from a table of daily records. The retraining job shuffles all rows randomly, puts 80% into training and 20% into the holdout, and the challenger always looks better than the champion; in production the new models often disappoint. Which change gives a more trustworthy selection?

choices.text: Increase the holdout to 50% of the rows while keeping the random shuffle, to reduce the variance of the estimate
Split by time, training on earlier days and evaluating on the most recent days, and score the champion on that same later period
Stratify the random split by product id, which keeps the same products in both parts
Normalize the holdout features with statistics computed on the holdout itself, so that its scale matches the production data at scoring time
