stem: A drift metrics table row for the column `plan_type` (a categorical feature with five values) shows `ks_test` as null, while `chi_squared_test` and `tv_distance` have values. A teammate suspects a bug in the profile. What is the correct reading?

choices.text: It is expected: the KS test is computed only for numeric columns, and categorical columns get chi-square, total variation and related distances
It means the column was converted to numbers by the profile, and the null shows that the KS test had too few distinct values to run on it
It means that `plan_type` has no drift, because null in a test column is how the table encodes the absence of any change
It is a bug, because the KS test is computed for every column type and a null value means that the refresh failed

stem: A numeric feature in a scoring table has about 400 million rows per window. The alert rule is `ks_test.pvalue < 0.05`, and it fires every day even though the distribution plots of the baseline and the current window look the same, and the model quality is unchanged. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Replace the KS test with a chi-square test on the same numeric column, because chi-square has no sensitivity to the sample size of a window
Lower the p-value limit to 0.0000001 and keep the rule otherwise unchanged, so that fewer days will fire
Alert on an effect size, such as the KS statistic, Wasserstein distance or PSI, against a threshold chosen for practical impact
Sample 100 rows per window so that the test has less power and stops detecting small differences

stem: A governance policy states that a numeric model input is considered significantly shifted when the population stability index against the baseline reaches a threshold. The team wants to align the alert with the guidance in the data profiling documentation. Which statement matches that guidance?

choices.text: A PSI below 0.05 is significant and a PSI near 1 means that the two distributions are identical
PSI of 0.2 or more is a significant change, 0.1 to below 0.2 moderate, and below 0.1 not significant
A PSI of 0.5 or more is significant, from 0.2 to below 0.5 is moderate, and everything below 0.2 means no change at all
PSI is a probability between 0 and 1 where 0.05 is the usual cutoff, as with a p-value

stem: A monitor tracks 300 numeric features with a KS test per feature on every refresh and alerts when any p-value is below 0.05. Even for stable data, about 15 features alarm per refresh and the on-call team ignores the alerts. Which approach reduces false alarms without ignoring real drift?

choices.text: Remove the 100 features with the highest variance, because noisy features are the source of false alarms
Raise the refresh frequency so that each alarm is checked twice, and ignore features that alarm only once
Alert only if the p-values of at least three consecutive days are below 0.05, and apply the same rule to all 300 features without any change
Correct for multiple comparisons (for example Bonferroni) or alert on effect-size thresholds, and prioritize features by importance

stem: Product wants a single drift rule for the categorical feature `device_type` that has a clear meaning for stakeholders: "alert when at least 5 percent of traffic has moved to different categories compared with the baseline". Which drift metric matches this wording most directly?

choices.text: `wasserstein_distance`, because it reports the share of categories whose frequency changed at all
`ks_test.statistic`, because the KS statistic always measures the share of rows that moved
`tv_distance` with a threshold of 0.05, the largest probability gap between the two distributions
`chi_squared_test.pvalue`, with the alert limit at 0.05, because 0.05 and 5 percent are the same number and the test measures the moved share

stem: A heavy-tailed numeric feature, `basket_value` in euros, shifts upward by about 12 euros on average after a pricing change. The team wants a drift number that says how far the distribution moved in the units of the feature, so that analysts can set the limit in euros. Which column of the drift metrics table fits?

choices.text: `ks_test.statistic`, because it is expressed in the units of the feature and equals the shift in the mean of the values
`percent_null_delta`, since a shift of values is a change in the share of non-null values
`chi_squared_test.statistic`, which is the same as the Wasserstein distance when the column is bucketed
`wasserstein_distance`, which is in the units of the feature and reads as the average distance moved

stem: A feature's mean rises by 0.3% every day, so each window differs only slightly from the previous one. After six weeks the distribution is far from the training data. The profile compares each window only to the previous one and no alert has fired. Which monitoring feature closes the gap?

choices.text: A baseline table with the training data, so that baseline drift measures every window against the fixed reference
A higher alert threshold on consecutive drift, so that the accumulated shift will show in the next window
A custom metric that stores yesterday's average, since the drift table cannot hold a value from before the previous window
A shorter window granularity such as one hour, because consecutive drift becomes sensitive to slow trends when windows are shorter

stem: An upstream outage made one daily window of a numeric feature look very different, and values returned to normal the next day. The team has alerts on both comparison types of the drift metrics table. The consecutive-drift alert fired on two days in a row, the baseline-drift alert on only one. How does this fit the two drift types?

choices.text: Consecutive drift compares each window with the first window ever profiled, so the return to normal differs from it as well
Consecutive drift compares a window with the previous one, so it fires into the anomaly and again on the return; baseline drift fires only in the window that differs
The profile writes every consecutive drift row twice, so the second alert is only a duplicate that the team can suppress by filtering on the window start time
Baseline drift is computed with a delay of one day, so it shows the outage a day late and never notices the return to normal

stem: Labels have arrived for last month's fraud scores. The fraud rate in the labelled data fell to a third of the usual value, feature drift against the baseline is small, ROC AUC is unchanged, but precision at the fixed alert threshold dropped sharply. Which interpretation and response fit best?

choices.text: The features must be corrupted, so retraining is pointless until the upstream pipeline is repaired, even though feature drift is small and the AUC is unchanged
An unchanged AUC proves that precision cannot have changed, so the precision metric of the profile is wrong and should be recomputed
The ranking is intact but the share of positives moved, so refit the threshold or the calibration on recent labelled data before considering a full retrain
Any precision change means the ranking has degraded as well, so the model must be retrained from scratch at once on the last month

stem: A credit model's input features show no drift against the baseline, yet default rates in a new segment behave differently from what the model learned, and its accuracy has fallen. Which statement about the monitoring explains this and names the setting that is needed?

choices.text: The baseline table must have been wrong; with the training data as baseline, the accuracy drop would have shown up as feature drift
Drift tests are flawed, because they compare only means; switching to a median-based test would have caught the accuracy loss
Accuracy cannot be tracked in a profile, so the team must compare predictions to labels in a separate notebook each month
The change is concept drift, which input tests cannot see; the inference profile needs the label column for accuracy metrics

stem: Labels for a recommendation model arrive about three weeks late, so quality metrics cannot be computed yet. The team still wants an early warning that the model's behavior has shifted. Which monitored column gives the earliest label-free evidence of model-level change?

choices.text: The prediction column, whose drift against the baseline is tracked daily without labels
The label column, because a profile can calculate drift on labels before they have been joined or are available
The model id column, because its distribution shows when a new version has been trained
The timestamp column, because a change in request timing proves that the model has changed

stem: A monitor on a low-traffic model uses hourly windows with about 150 requests each and alerts on KS p-values. Alerts flap every few hours, and the distribution plots across days look steady. Which change fits the traffic?

choices.text: Add a second profile with the same hourly granularity, because two profiles halve the noise in the alerts
Use a daily (or longer) window so each window has enough rows, and alert on an effect size with a threshold
Use a shorter granularity of five minutes, so each alert is based on the freshest requests
Switch the alert from the drift table to the profile metrics table, because it is unaffected by window size
